name: Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia type II (SEC23B)
aliases: hereditary erythroblastic multinuclearity with positive acidified serum test

clinicalPearls: The commonest congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, autosomal recessive and caused by biallelic SEC23B mutations
Historically termed HEMPAS: hereditary erythroblastic multinuclearity with a positive acidified serum (Ham) test
Marrow shows characteristic bi- and multinucleate late erythroblasts
Red cells lyse in acidified normal sera due to an unusual membrane antigen, but the patient's own serum does not lyse them (unlike paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria)
Band 3 (the anion exchanger) shows a distinctive narrow, faster-migrating band with hypoglycosylation on SDS-PAGE of the red-cell membrane
Presentation ranges from mild to transfusion-dependent anaemia with jaundice, splenomegaly, and gallstones
Iron overload develops from ineffective erythropoiesis, independent of transfusion
Diagnosis is confirmed by SEC23B genetic testing, supported by marrow morphology and membrane protein studies
reference.pathophysiology: SEC23B encodes a component of the COPII vesicle coat that transports cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi. Biallelic loss of function impairs glycoprotein trafficking and glycosylation during erythroid maturation, producing abnormal, hypoglycosylated band 3 and other membrane proteins and the aberrant surface antigen responsible for the positive acidified-serum test. Disordered maturation yields bi- and multinucleated erythroblasts and marked intramedullary destruction (ineffective erythropoiesis); the chronic anaemia suppresses hepcidin and drives progressive iron overload.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary spherocytosis and other membrane disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count showing anaemia with inadequate reticulocytosis
Bone marrow aspirate demonstrating bi- and multinucleate erythroblasts
Acidified-serum (Ham) test using compatible normal sera, with the patient's own serum as control
SDS-PAGE of red-cell membrane proteins showing the abnormal band 3 pattern
Iron studies to assess overload and genetic testing for SEC23B
Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins to exclude paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
redFlags: Progressive iron overload with cardiac, hepatic, or endocrine complications
Transfusion dependence or severe symptomatic anaemia
Aplastic crisis, for example following parvovirus B19 infection
Features suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria
reference.prognosis: Severity varies widely; milder cases have a near-normal life expectancy, but transfusion dependence and, more importantly, cumulative iron overload determine long-term outcome unless iron status is monitored and managed.
pitfalls: Confusing the positive acidified-serum test with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, which is excluded by flow cytometry and by the negative reaction with the patient's own serum
Overlooking non-transfusional iron overload and failing to monitor it
Misinterpreting the dyserythropoietic marrow as myelodysplasia
Delaying genetic confirmation when morphology and membrane studies are already suggestive
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Iron chelation with deferasirox, deferiprone or desferrioxamine is the therapeutic mainstay, as progressive iron overload develops from suppressed hepcidin even without transfusion
Give folic acid supplementation to sustain chronic ineffective erythropoiesis
Reserve leucodepleted, phenotype-matched red-cell transfusion for symptomatic or transfusion-dependent anaemia
Consider splenectomy to reduce haemolysis and transfusion need, with prior vaccination against encapsulated organisms and awareness of thrombotic risk
Monitor ferritin and hepatic and cardiac iron by MRI, and screen for pigment gallstones and jaundice
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing for autosomal recessive SEC23B inheritance
Refer to specialist haematology and consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in severe childhood disease
